buckets.title: Rational numbers in the real-number system
buckets.badge_reason: The bounded demand is recognizing a universal set-inclusion statement and using one counterexample to reject narrower sets.

capabilities.action: Classify a rational number by using set inclusion and boundary counterexamples to distinguish rational, real, integer, whole and natural membership.
capabilities.success_criterion: Correctly states that every rational number is real and can reject integer, whole or natural as universal supersets by giving a rational counterexample such as 1/2.

microtopics.title: Use rational-number set inclusion and a boundary example
microtopics.badge_reason: The key move is conceptual rather than computational: interpret “every” as set inclusion, then test narrower alternatives with a rational counterexample.
entry_assumptions: Can recognize a fraction such as 1/2 as a rational number.
microtopics.inferential_jump: A universal membership claim can be settled by combining the inclusion Q ⊂ R with one rational counterexample that lies outside the narrower natural, whole and integer sets.

teaching_path.action: Read “every rational number is …” as a claim that the entire rational set must sit inside the chosen set.
teaching_path.why_valid: The word every makes the statement universal, so the chosen target set must contain all rational numbers.
teaching_path.output: a set-inclusion test rather than an example-matching test

teaching_path.action: Use 1/2 as a boundary example to test the natural, whole and integer choices.
teaching_path.why_valid: One counterexample is enough to disprove a universal set-membership statement.
teaching_path.output: natural, whole and integer are rejected as universal supersets of the rationals

teaching_path.action: Check the remaining real-number claim against the inclusion Q ⊂ R.
teaching_path.why_valid: Every rational number is a real number, so the universal statement holds.
teaching_path.output: real number is the valid universal classification

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A familiar rational example being an integer means every rational number is an integer.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Does 1/2 belong to the integers, whole numbers or natural numbers?
misconceptions.repair: Use 1/2 as a counterexample: it is rational but belongs to none of those three narrower sets.

exit_task.prompt: Explain why 3/4 is a real number but not an integer, whole number or natural number.

answer.summary: 3/4 is rational and therefore real, but it is not an integer, whole number or natural number.
reasoning: 3/4 is a ratio of integers with non-zero denominator, so it is rational.
3/4 is not an integer, so it is also not whole or natural.
answer.check: The classification must include rational and real while excluding integer, whole and natural.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The task is a set-membership explanation, not a computed numerical claim.

microtopics.research_contribution: Provides the smallest authored explanatory bridge needed to support the verified source question while keeping source wording and authored pedagogy separate.

question_families.title: Rational-number set-classification practice
solution_structure: Use a boundary rational number to reject narrower sets.
Confirm the surviving claim with Q ⊂ R.

demand_dimensions.model_choice: Choose set inclusion rather than arithmetic calculation as the governing model.
demand_dimensions.representation_translation: Translate verbal membership language into nested number-set relations.
demand_dimensions.reasoning_steps: Move from universal claim to counterexample test to final inclusion check.
demand_dimensions.novelty: Vary the rational example or the candidate target sets without changing the inclusion logic.

safe_variations: Replace 1/2 with another non-integer rational such as 3/4.
Ask which listed sets must contain every rational number.
transfer_boundaries: Do not infer integer, whole or natural membership merely because some rationals lie in those sets.
Do not treat irrational-number classification as the same family; it changes the source set.
common_wrong_routes: Choose integer because many familiar rational examples are integers.
Choose whole or natural without testing a non-integer rational.

questions.stem: Classify 3/4 among the natural, whole, integer, rational and real number sets. Explain one boundary example or set-inclusion fact that justifies your classification.
conditions: Use standard school definitions of the listed number sets.

answer.summary: 3/4 is rational and real, but not integer, whole or natural.
reasoning: 3/4 is a ratio of two integers with non-zero denominator, so it is rational.
Because 3/4 is not an integer, it is not whole or natural.

reasoning_route.action: Treat 3/4 as an example whose set memberships must be checked.
reasoning_route.why_valid: The prompt asks for classification across nested number sets.

reasoning_route.action: Use the definition of rational number and Q ⊂ R.
reasoning_route.why_valid: 3/4 is a ratio of integers and every rational is real.
Whole and natural numbers are integer subsets, so non-integer status excludes all three.

answer.check: A correct response includes rational and real, excludes integer/whole/natural, and gives a set-membership reason.

hints.text: Start by asking whether 3/4 can be written as p/q with integers p and q≠0.
After deciding it is rational, use the nesting of number sets to decide which broader set must also contain it.

scaffolds.text: Write two columns: sets that contain 3/4 and sets that do not.
Use Q ⊂ R after you establish rational membership.

difficulty.basis: One set-inclusion decision plus one boundary check; no algebraic computation is required.
